subtype: Approach: builds a detailed plan for months ahead and delays starting [Pitfall]
passage:
Day 15. Finally finished the semester timetable. Six colours, one for each subject, pale grey for revision, and a thick border round exam days. I redid it twice because the yellow looked wrong. It is beautiful.
Started actual studying an hour ago and then looked at the calendar. The first internal test is nine days away, not the twenty-four I had counted in my head. Two weeks gone.
The timetable has slots for everything except catching up. I haven't opened a single unit since the first lecture. Going to read Unit 1 tonight, and Unit 2 in the morning, before classes.
Vishal

qa.q: How many colours are on the timetable?
qa.a: There are six colours, one for each subject, plus pale grey for revision.

qa.q: What did Vishal feel on looking at the calendar after starting to study?
qa.a: Vishal felt shocked and behind, since the first test is nine days away, not twenty-four.

qa.q: What different approach could Vishal use now?
qa.a: Vishal could plan only the days before the test and start reading at once, since a small plan gets studying going without more delay.

qa.q: How might Vishal's teacher see the beautiful timetable if the test goes badly?
qa.a: The teacher would probably see that the preparation started late, and that the time spent on the chart is the cost, not a sign of hard studying.

grounding: A student spends two weeks colour-coding a semester timetable, then starts studying with less time left.
